# SK2143 — Two arguments are passed crosswise to the parameters they are named after

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

Two adjacent arguments of the same type are named after the two parameters they fill, in the opposite order.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S2234 |

## Why

Two parameters of the same type next to each other are the one place a transposed call compiles and runs. Nothing at the call site marks it, the types agree, the tests that pass both values through symmetric code stay green, and the failure surfaces somewhere else entirely. The only evidence available is the names: when the argument sitting in `destination` is a variable called `source` and the argument sitting in `source` is called `destination`, the author's own naming says which way round they meant it and the call says the other.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
void Copy(string source, string destination) { }

void Run(string source, string destination) {
    Copy(destination, source);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
void Copy(string source, string destination) { }

void Run(string source, string destination) {
    Copy(source, destination);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **`Copy(source, destination)` called as `Copy(destination, source)` is undetectable in general, and this rule does not try.** The only sound signal is a *crosswise name match*: two **adjacent** parameters of the **same** type, filled by two plain identifiers whose own names are the two parameter names, swapped. Everything looser reports ordinary code, so everything looser is declined — non-adjacent pairs, differing parameter types, member accesses, calls, literals and any expression that is not a bare identifier. ⚠ **Names shorter than three characters are ignored.** `Max(y, x)` and `Add(b, a)` are the shapes where reversal is deliberate and a one-letter name carries no evidence about intent at all. ⚠ **A call to a method of the same name as the enclosing member is declined**, which is the guard for the deliberate reversal that does exist and is correct: a descending comparer written as `Compare(right, left)` delegating to another `Compare` is exactly the crosswise shape and exactly not a defect. ⚠ **Type parameters are excluded** — two `T` arguments to a generic helper are the same case with none of the evidence. The call must supply exactly as many arguments as the method has parameters, with no named arguments, no `ref`/`out` and no `params` expansion, so that "the parameter this argument fills" is a fact rather than an inference. The fix swaps the two expressions and is **not** safe to apply unreviewed — the whole finding is a question about intent, and the rule is wrong about it in exactly the cases where the author meant the reversal.
